CSS decides how a page looks: colors, sizes, spacing and layout. Most CSS confusion comes from two questions: which rule wins, and how big is this box. Answer those, and the rest is looking up properties.

A Rule

.card {
  padding: 16px;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 8px;
}

A rule is a selector (.card), then declarations: a property and a value. Add CSS in a .css file linked from the page's head with <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css" />.

Selectors

Selector Matches
p Every p element
.card Elements with class="card"
#header The element with id="header"
.card p p anywhere inside a .card
.card > p p directly inside a .card
a:hover A link under the mouse
input:focus The input with keyboard focus
li:first-child The first li of its list
[type="email"] Elements with that attribute value

Style with classes in almost all cases. They're reusable and have a moderate weight, which keeps the next topic simple.

The Cascade: Which Rule Wins?

When several rules set the same property on the same element, the browser picks one:

  1. Specificity: the more specific selector wins. Roughly, an ID beats classes, and classes beat element names.
  2. Order: with equal specificity, the rule written later wins.
Selector Weight (IDs, classes, elements)
p 0, 0, 1
.card p 0, 1, 1
.card .title 0, 2, 0
#main .title 1, 1, 0

So .card .title { color: red } beats .title { color: blue }, wherever they are in the file.

Avoid IDs for styling and !important: both win so strongly that you need even stronger rules to override them later. Keep selectors short and flat.

Inheritance

Some properties, mostly text ones like color, font-family and line-height, are inherited by children. Set them once on body, and everything follows. Box properties like padding and border aren't inherited.

The Box Model

Every element is a box made of four layers:

┌───────────── margin ─────────────┐
│ ┌────────── border ────────────┐ │
│ │ ┌──────── padding ─────────┐ │ │
│ │ │        content           │ │ │
│ │ └──────────────────────────┘ │ │
│ └──────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
  • content: the text or image.
  • padding: space inside the border, with the background color.
  • border: the line around it.
  • margin: space outside, between this box and others.

box-sizing: border-box

By default, width sets only the content. A box with width: 300px, padding: 20px and a 1px border is really 342px wide. That's rarely what you want, so almost every project starts with:

*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

Now width: 300px means the whole box, padding and border included.

Margin Collapse

The vertical margins of two blocks one above the other collapse: a 20px bottom margin meeting a 30px top margin gives 30px, not 50px. It surprises everyone once. Flexbox and grid gaps don't collapse, which is one reason to prefer gap for spacing.

display

  • block: takes the full width and starts on a new line, like div, p and h1.
  • inline: flows inside text, like a, strong and span. Width, height and vertical margins don't apply.
  • inline-block: flows inline, but accepts width, height and padding.
  • flex and grid: turn the element into a layout container for its children. That's how most layouts are built today; practice them in the Flexbox & Grid Playground.
  • none: hides the element completely.

Units

Unit Relative to Good for
px Nothing (fixed) Borders, small details
rem The root font size (often 16px) Font sizes, spacing
em The element's own font size Spacing that grows with the text
% The parent's size Fluid widths
vw / vh 1% of the viewport's width / height Full-screen sections
fr Free space in a grid Grid columns

Prefer rem for font sizes: if a user sets a larger default font in their browser, your whole page scales with it. 1.5rem is 24px with the default settings. For responsive font sizes, clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem) grows with the screen between a minimum and a maximum.

Colors

color: #1f2937;
color: rgb(31 41 55);
color: rgb(31 41 55 / 50%); /* half transparent */

Keep enough contrast between text and background: at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text, so it stays readable for everyone.

The Answer in Short

  1. A rule is a selector plus declarations; style mostly with classes.
  2. The more specific selector wins, and with equal specificity the later one; avoid IDs and !important.
  3. Every box is content, padding, border and margin; use box-sizing: border-box.
  4. display decides how a box flows; use flexbox and grid for layouts.
  5. Use rem for text and spacing, % and fr for fluid layouts, px for small details.
